title: Missing Hours
logline: A calculating player enters a hyper-realistic 1984 Vermont battle royale to solve its hidden ritual and win a life-changing prize, treating every host as a renewable resource — until the missing hours start to stick.
premise: The Analyst enters a closed hyper-real battle royale rendered as 1984 Bennington with one plan: decode the Daywalker Ritual, avoid early messy conflict, and take the prize by treating Hosts as renewable resources. He maps branching paths and drains three Hosts in rotation so they regenerate, while five rival Guests rewrite the town around him as world-state pressure. The Psychologist's hypnosis of Host deception networks collides with his calculated feeding; the Memory Wipe, the failsafe against existential collapse, begins to leak. A night-shift Host collects polaroids and cassette fragments of hours she cannot remember, and the Analyst must use her investigation even as he becomes its subject. The story proves that treating a mind as a system to be solved creates a debt no reset can cancel: someone chooses, and pays in something that cannot be wiped.

audience.reader_promise: A want-versus-need climax and a payment the Memory Wipe cannot touch — neither a win screen nor a sermon.

setting.period: Diegetic 1984; extra-diegetic near-future closed VR match
places: Downtown Bennington, Vermont — Main Street, diner, arcade, hardware store
Bennington College campus and its party houses
The hospital and the police station
The deep woods and a programmed hunting ground
Night rooms where analog memory is made: photo lab, radio booth, diner
rules_of_the_world: The match is closed. Guests cannot log out, reach an operator, or leave town. Elimination or completion of the Daywalker Ritual are the only exits. One prize.
Guests spawn in period-accurate 1984 clothing with exactly one hundred dollars and no inventory. Everything else must be found, bought, stolen, or made inside the town.
Guests are vampires inside the match. They must feed on Host blood. Hunger is physiological and escalating: unfed Guests weaken, then frenzy, then die. Frenzy is visible and destroys strategy.

Feeding has a hard limit. A Host drained past a recoverable threshold dies permanently for the match and does not respawn. A Host drained short of that threshold regenerates blood over hours but keeps somatic marks and affective residue.

Guest powers are only these: feeding; short-range hypnosis that writes to a Host's deception networks; modest physical enhancement; night-vision. Sunlight and UV, including hardware-store UV lamps, injure Guests. Mirrors do not expose them. No other supernatural permissions exist.

The Daywalker Ritual is the win condition. It requires a finite, locatable set of tokens and a dawn invocation at one fixed site in town. Completing it makes that Guest immune to sun and ends the match in their favor. Tokens cannot be spawned or wished into being.

Hosts are neuro-cognitive models with authentic emotional regulation, the capacity to lie, and working deception networks. They are not scripts. They form attachments, hold grudges, investigate anomalies, and protect each other.

The Memory Wipe: every time a Host sleeps, autobiographical memory since the previous waking is erased. Semantic skill and personality persist. Affective residue and somatic marks bleed through the seam. Facts do not. The wipe is automatic and cannot be selectively edited by Guests.

If a Host reaches a stable, evidence-backed belief that they are inside a simulation, the model undergoes existential collapse — catatonia, uncontrolled affect, or self-destruction. The Memory Wipe is the designed failsafe. Persistent objects — polaroids, cassette recordings, handwriting, newsprint — can carry facts across a wipe and are therefore dangerous to the failsafe.

Hypnosis can implant a false memory or suppress a true one until the next sleep. It does not survive a wipe unless the Host is kept awake or the write is continuously re-implanted. Stacked or contradictory hypnotic writes destabilize the emotional-regulation network.

The awakening glitch requires both (a) the Psychologist's repeated hypnotic writes to deception networks and (b) the Analyst's rotational draining of the same Hosts. Either alone is insufficient. After the glitch, wipes become incomplete: fragments of declarative memory persist, and Hosts can compare notes.
Rival Guests alter the world-state whether or not they appear on-screen. Their tactics stay consistent with their dossiers and cannot be retconned for convenience.

The town is geographically closed by fog and a road that loops. No one arrives from outside. No one leaves. Period radio, television, and newspapers are generated texture and carry no real-world news.

In-match death of a Guest is elimination: they vanish and leave no body. In-match death of a Host leaves a body. Ur-Vampires in the woods are programmed predators, not Guests; eating an Ur-Vampire heart permanently raises a Guest's physical stats.

Nothing that a camera could not photograph and a microphone could not hear is a fact of the world. Glitches manifest as analog artifacts — roll-bar, tape-smear, wrong shadows — never as floating UI, health bars, waypoints, or chat windows.

must_include: Exactly three plots: the external game the Analyst is solving; the town waking up; his internal collapse from detachment into moral reckoning
The Psychologist's interference as the causal bridge from the game plot to the awakening plot, conjoined with the Analyst's rotational drains
Memory Wipe obeyed in exact terms in every scene that touches sleep, hypnosis, or recollection
Daywalker Ritual as a decodeable win condition with finite tokens and one dawn site
Analyst competence and clean early feeding shown before any moral collapse
At least one fully realized Host with her own ruling passion, inner conflict, and agency — not a device for his education
Polaroids and at least one cassette that persist across wipes and pay off
Five rival Guests as world-state pressure, largely off-screen
Hunger as a ticking clock that worsens when scenes would otherwise sag
An ending that is a choice and a payment in something that cannot be reset
must_avoid: On-the-nose philosophy or any character explaining consciousness
Explicit sexual content; keep implication and fade
A simple victory ending or a simple condemnation ending
Hosts used only to educate the Analyst
Villain motives for the Psychologist, the town, or the rivals when a human one will do
Breaking Memory Wipe, feeding thresholds, or Ritual rules for convenience
On-screen rival showdowns that turn the piece into an action ensemble
The Analyst quitting, taking a bribe, or walking away — he is steadfast
Idiot-in-the-attic choices; every principal at maximum capacity

keep_in_mind: CORE CONFLICT: the Analyst's insistence on solving the simulation and taking the prize versus the Hosts' emerging claim to be minds rather than resources — mastery against recognition.

CRUCIBLE: Guests cannot log out; hunger escalates toward frenzy or death; only one prize exists; fog and the looping road lock everyone in town. The Analyst cannot abandon the Host he has damaged because her surviving knowledge is now the only practical path through the Ritual, and leaving her to the other Guests would finish the thing he is beginning to find intolerable.
Frey premise, exactly one: Treating a mind as a system to be solved leads to a debt that no reset can cancel.
Want versus need: his conscious want is to complete the Ritual and take the prize; his unconscious need is to recognize one particular mind as real. The climax forces the choice. He cannot have both.

Growth axis, pole to pole: detached systems-thinker → a man who cannot unsee a particular face. Every complication must move him measurably along this axis; his response to conflict must change as he moves.
Begin before the beginning. Status quo first: mapping, clean rotational feeding, small tactical wins. Only then break it. Detachment must read as competence so that its collapse costs something.

Causal link is mandatory and double: the Psychologist's stacked hypnotic writes plus the Analyst's rotational drains. Neither alone wakes the town. Plot 1 produces Plot 2 only through that conjunction.

The Host is a full character. Give her a ruling passion that is not him, an inner conflict of her own (know versus sleep; expose versus stay sane), and agency that alters the world-state without his permission. Camera may sit with her actions and objects; do not grant interior monologue.

Rivals remain mostly off-screen. Register them as consequences: barricaded sectors and UV shop-lights (Architect), dry hospital blood and tribute talk (Syndicate), a college cult of willing donors (Hedonist), a heartless body at the treeline (Hunter), Hosts who insist on memories they should not have (Psychologist).

Plant by scene three, unremarked, the thing that cannot be reset — an object, a recording, a kept hour, a name. Conspicuous plants must fire. Polaroids, one cassette, fog-as-static, CRT roll-bar, and the seam are the motif set.

Equalize forces. The waking town wants not to be eaten and not to forget. The Psychologist is testing whether a simulated mind can hold a lie across a wipe — a research question, not sadism. Never give either a villain's motive.

Dual character: a cold tactician and a man capable of recognition occupy one body. Fastidious small manners (he pays, he tips, he returns what he did not mean to take) begin as control and become the leak. Force the two states to collide.
Conflict must rise slowly, not static and not jumping. Escalation is character change. Default to the harder honest option. Scene outcomes: no, yes-but, or no-and-worse.

Externalize everything. A decision is a bag set down, a tape pressed into a hand, a coat left on a hook, a polaroid withheld. Subtext in every scene of consequence. Facts arrive as weapons, never as briefings.

Philosophy arrives only as situation. Sexuality and violence belong to the world and are felt; implication does the work. The ending is neither victory nor sermon: someone chooses, and pays in the planted thing the wipe cannot touch.
